newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Senate report blasts banks, seeks overhaul.
newsitem.headline: French Senate report blasts banks, seeks overhaul.

text.p: The French banking system has suffered years of tactical and strategic error by the banks themselves and mishandling by the state and should be thoroughly overhauled, a Senate report released on Tuesday said.
It urged reform of bank law, ending competitive distortions, and state withdrawal from the competitive banking sector.
"The banking sector has gone through a crisis without precedent," a summary of the report said.

"Despite a recent improvement, French banks are still less profitable than their international rivals," which is shackling development, leaving them open to downgrading by rating agencies and technically vulnerable to takeover, it said.
The report says the banks committed "tactical or strategic management errors" and also lays the blame for the sector's woes on the state itself.
"The state-as-banker is a bad shareholder and a bad manager," says the report.
"It knows no other way of dealing with banking crises than systematically arranging for the recapitalisation of failing credit establishments," it says.

"We therefore need to re-examine the banking risk system so that it is not turned into a 'life insurance' policy for all institutions and also to prepare the withdrawal of the state from the competitive sector."

"In the case of state-controlled banks, the state should stop looking on recapitalisation as the only way to sort out their problems. Sale or liquidiation should be looked to more often, for small and big institutions alike," says the report.
"This is the price of a healthy (banking) sector."
"Secondly, there should be a withdrawal from the market of establishments which have the benefits of marketplace support and systems guaranteeing deposits," says the report.
It says the sector failed to restructure amid sea changes in international banking in the 1980s, sharing the burden instead of adapting by cutting staff and letting the weakest disappear.
The report says huge and repeated state intervention to help state banks added to the problem of a sector where players were free to enter but only few made an exit, creating overcapacity.

"Under increasing competitive pressure, the banks committed tactical and or strategic errors," it said, citing "collective blindness" on the risks of hefty property investment by many banks before the bottom fell out of the property market.
The situation was exacerbated by the government handing out special public service mandates to banks to underpin industrial policy, the report says.
Banks also had to bear the burden of too much taxation in tough times and found it harder to change when long term interest rates fell below short term rates between 1989 and 1994, the report says.

The reports says the sector is marred by competitive distortions such as monopolies for selling certain popular savings schemes, differences of statutes between financial institutions and differing tax and work time laws.

It suggests getting rid of a 1937 decree which limits branch opening times for commercial banks but not for others in the sector, greater harmonisation of tax law across the sector and changing the statutes of the Caisse d'Epargne savings bank grouping as well as the post office, La Poste.
